subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the circles x² + y² − 6x − 9y + 13 = 0 and x² + y² − 2x − 16y = 0 touch each other. Find the point of contact and the equation of the common tangent at that point.

mark_split.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
Centre and radius of the second circle

insider_note: This is the mirror image of the external case: C₁C₂ = r₂ − r₁ means internal touching, and internal touching means the contact point divides C₁C₂ EXTERNALLY — the two words swap over, which is the whole difficulty of the pair.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
steps.margin_note: One mark. The y coefficient is odd, so f = −9/2 and the radius carries a fraction. Keep everything over 4.
steps.memory_tip: An odd coefficient of y gives a half in f. Put the whole radius over the denominator 4 before taking the root.
steps.why: Comparing with the general form gives 2f = −9, so f = −9/2. Writing 9 and 13 over 4 as 36/4 and 52/4 lets the whole expression be squared and rooted in one step.
common_mistakes: Taking f = −9 and getting a radius of √77.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the second circle
steps.margin_note: Second mark. There is no constant term, so c = 0 — the circle passes through the origin.
steps.memory_tip: No constant term means c = 0, and then the circle goes through the origin.
steps.why: A missing constant term means c = 0. The radius is then √(g² + f²), and here it comes out as √65 — exactly twice the first radius, which is what makes the touching exact.
common_mistakes: Inventing a constant term because the equation looks incomplete.

steps.label: Show that the circles touch
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Compare with the DIFFERENCE of the radii here, and take the larger radius first so the difference is positive.
steps.memory_tip: Difference of the radii equals the distance between the centres: one circle sits inside the other.
lines: ∴ The circles touch each other internally.
steps.why: When the distance between the centres equals the difference of the radii, the smaller circle lies inside the larger one and they meet at exactly one point. Here 9/2 − 8 = −7/2, and its square is 49/4.
common_mistakes: Comparing with r₁ + r₂ and concluding the circles do not touch.
Writing r₁ − r₂, which is negative and cannot equal a distance.

steps.label: Find the point of contact
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Internal touching uses the EXTERNAL division formula, with the minus sign in the denominator.
steps.memory_tip: The contact point lies beyond one centre, not between them, so the division is external.
lines: P divides C₁C₂ externally in the ratio 1 : 2
steps.why: For internal touching the smaller circle is inside the larger, so the contact point lies on the line of centres but outside the segment joining them. That is external division in the ratio r₁ : r₂.

steps.label: Find the common tangent
steps.margin_note: The last mark. The second circle has no constant term, so nothing is subtracted from the constant of the first.
steps.memory_tip: The common tangent at the point of contact is S − S′ = 0, for internal touching as well.
lines: The common tangent at the point of contact
steps.why: S − S′ = 0 works for both kinds of touching, because it is the one line that meets both circles at their single shared point. A check: 4(5) − 7(1) − 13 = 0, so P lies on it.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as −4x + 7y + 13 = 0, which is correct but usually written with a positive leading coefficient.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. Draw it in rough to see that P lies beyond C₁, the smaller circle's centre, not between the centres.
steps.memory_tip: One circle inside the other, touching at one point. Going along the line of centres the order is C₂, then C₁, then P, so the division is external.
steps.why: The picture shows why the section formula changes. With the small circle inside the large one, the contact point P is not between C₁ and C₂ — it lies beyond C₁, on the far side from C₂ — so the division must be external. The common tangent is again the line through P at right angles to C₁C₂.
common_mistakes: Drawing the circles side by side, which is the external case and gives the wrong point.
Placing the contact point between the two centres.
